Abstract
Objective  Anoikis, a form of programmed cell death triggered by detachment 
from the extracellular matrix, plays a crucial role in metastasis and immune escape in 
melanoma. We aimed to identify anoikis-related prognostic markers using integrated 
machine learning and single-cell analysis.
Methods  We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing data from the GEO dataset 
GSE215120 and transcriptomic profiles from multiple melanoma cohorts, including 
TCGA, GSE19234, GSE22153, and GSE65904. Batch effects in single-cell data were 
corrected using the Harmony algorithm. Cell subpopulations were annotated via 
t-SNE dimensionality reduction and canonical markers, and AUCell was employed to 
compute the enrichment scores of anoikis-related genes across cell subtypes. A total 
of 150 anoikis-related genes were identified, and 101 machine learning algorithms 
and their combinations (including Cox regression, random survival forest, and 
gradient boosting machine) were systematically evaluated to identify the optimal 
prognostic model. Model performance was validated in independent cohorts using 
the concordance index (C-index), Kaplan–Meier survival analysis, and time-dependent 
ROC curves. Tumor microenvironment characteristics were assessed using ESTIMATE, 
CIBERSORT, and GSVA. The clinical relevance and functional role of SLC3A2 were further 
validated using the BEST database and in vitro experiments, including shRNA-mediated 
knockdown, colony formation, and Transwell migration assays.
Results  Single-cell analysis revealed significantly elevated anoikis scores in endothelial 
cells, fibroblasts, and melanocytes. High-scoring subpopulations exhibited more 
active cell–cell communication networks centered on endothelial cells. The “random 
survival forest + gradient boosting machine” model demonstrated optimal prognostic 
performance across the TCGA training cohort and validation cohorts (GSE19234, 
GSE22153, GSE65904), with a C-index of 0.774. Patients in the high-risk group had 
significantly shorter overall survival, and the model achieved strong predictive 
accuracy with AUCs ranging from 0.64 to 0.81 for 1-, 3-, and 5-year survival. Tumor 
microenvironment analysis indicated reduced immune infiltration (CD8⁺ T cells, B cells) 
in the high-risk group, suggestive of an immunosuppressive phenotype. SLC3A2 was

1  Introduction
Melanoma is a malignant tumor originating from skin melanocytes [1–3]. In recent 
years, its incidence has significantly increased, and it has a high potential for metasta­
sis [4]. Despite the progress made in immunotherapy and targeted therapies, melanoma 
treatment still faces significant challenges, particularly in advanced cases [5]. The indi­
vidual differences in treatment responses and the emergence of resistance to malignant 
tumors make it necessary for researchers to develop new prediction tools and therapeu­
tic strategies to improve patient survival and quality of life [6]. Therefore, identifying key 
biomarkers related to the occurrence and progression of melanoma, along with their 
potential mechanisms, has become one of the hot topics in current cancer research.
In recent years, apoptosis research has gradually gained widespread attention, espe­
cially the study of “anoikis,” a specific form of programmed cell death that occurs when 
cells lose contact with the extracellular matrix (ECM) [7–9]. Anoikis plays a crucial role 
in maintaining tissue homeostasis and tumor metastasis [10]. Normal cells undergo 
anoikis when detached from the ECM, leading to self-destruction, whereas tumor cells 
escape this process, enabling their invasive growth and metastatic ability [11]. Studies 
have shown that anoikis is closely related to tumor invasiveness and metastasis, playing a 
vital role in the progression of many cancers, including melanoma.
Cellular heterogeneity in melanoma is one of the key factors contributing to the dif­
ficulty in treatment [12]. Different tumor cell populations may exhibit significant dif­
ferences in gene expression, immune evasion, drug response, and other aspects [13]. 
Therefore, revealing the gene expression characteristics and functional states of different 
subpopulations of melanoma cells is of great significance for understanding the biologi­
cal characteristics of the tumor. The advent of single-cell RNA sequencing technology 
has provided a powerful tool for in-depth analysis of tumor cell heterogeneity. Through 
single-cell RNA sequencing, we can explore gene expression patterns of different cell 
populations in the tumor microenvironment at the single-cell level and reveal their 
interactions.
In this study, we used single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data and large-scale 
tumor sample RNA-sequencing data, combined with gene set enrichment analysis 
(GSEA) and other methods, to explore the expression profiles of genes related to anoikis 
in melanoma and their correlation with clinical prognosis. We constructed a prognostic 
model based on 101 different machine learning algorithms and their combinations, and 
validated its predictive ability in multiple independent melanoma cohorts. Through this 
approach, we aim to provide new predictive tools for melanoma clinical treatment and 
potential biomarkers for future targeted therapies.

Conclusion  This study highlights the pivotal role of anoikis resistance in melanoma 
heterogeneity and immune microenvironment remodeling. The machine learning–
based prognostic model we constructed holds clinical translational potential, and 
SLC3A2 was validated as a potential therapeutic target, offering new strategies for 
precision treatment of melanoma.

With the increasing application of machine learning in the biomedical field, many 
studies have begun to combine different machine learning algorithms to build prognos­
tic models for tumors. These models can comprehensively assess multiple factors, accu­
rately evaluate patient survival risk, and predict their treatment response. In particular, 
gene expression-based predictive models have become an important direction in cancer 
biomarker research. However, despite these advances, selecting the appropriate algo­
rithm and evaluation criteria to construct a prognostic model with clinical application 
value remains a topic worthy of in-depth exploration.
This study combines various advanced bioinformatics technologies, integrating the in-
depth analysis of anoikis-related genes and machine learning algorithms, to construct a 
novel prognostic model for melanoma. We validated the model’s effectiveness using data 
from different clinical cohorts and public databases. The results show that the model 
effectively distinguishes high-risk and low-risk groups of melanoma patients and pro­
vides a reference for individualized treatment strategies.
Through the analysis and functional studies of different cell populations in melanoma, 
we further revealed the potential role of anoikis in the tumor microenvironment, espe­
cially its relationship with tumor immune evasion and metastasis. This provides new 
insights into exploring the immune evasion mechanisms and therapeutic strategies for 
melanoma. We hope that the findings of this study will provide new biomarkers for clini­
cal use and open new pathways for the precise treatment of melanoma.
2  Materials and methods
2.1  Data Acquisition and Processing
The single-cell RNA sequencing dataset of melanoma (GSE215120) and the bulk RNA-
sequencing datasets from melanoma patients (GSE19234, GSE22153, and GSE65904) 
were downloaded from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database ​(​h​t​t​p​s​:​/​/​w​w​w​.​n​
c​b​i​.​n​l​m​.​n​i​h​.​g​o​v​/​g​e​o​/​) [14–17]. RNA-sequencing data and clinical survival information 
for the melanoma cohort from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) were obtained from 
the TCGA database (​h​t​t​p​s​:​/​/​w​w​w​.​c​a​n​c​e​r​.​g​o​v​/​c​c​g​/​r​e​s​e​a​r​c​h​/​g​e​n​o​m​e​-​s​e​q​u​e​n​c​i​n​g​/​t​c​g​a). 
For the single-cell RNA-sequencing data, we selected 6 patients with acral melanoma 
because these samples had a higher cell count and better sequencing results. Quality 
control was first performed, including filtering based on the number of genes expressed 
and the proportion of mitochondrial gene content [18]. Batch effects were then removed 
using the Harmony integration algorithm. The data was dimensionally reduced using 
the umap and tsne methods. Finally, the results of the tsne method were presented, and 
annotations were made based on the markers of each cell. For the bulk RNA-sequencing 
datasets, batch effects were removed using the “sva” R package, and the data were log2-
transformed prior to downstream analysis. Anoikis-related genes were obtained from 
the GeneCards database.
2.2  Single-Cell Analysis of Anoikis-Related Gene Enrichment
Following dimensionality reduction and clustering of the single-cell RNA sequencing 
data, the AUCell package was used to calculate the enrichment scores of anoikis-related 
genes across different cellular subpopulations, and the results were visualized accord­
ingly. Based on the median anoikis enrichment score, cells were stratified into high- and 
low-score groups. Differences in intercellular communication between the two groups

were evaluated using the CellChat R package. Finally, Pearson correlation analysis was 
performed to identify genes strongly associated with the anoikis score, and the top 150 
genes were selected for further downstream analysis.
2.3  Construction of a Prognostic Model Using 101 Machine Learning Algorithms and Their 
Combinations
After identifying 150 anoikis-related genes, we constructed prognostic models by sys­
tematically integrating 101 machine learning algorithms and their pairwise combina­
tions. The detailed algorithms and modeling procedures can be found in the study 
by our previously published work [19]. The TCGA melanoma cohort was used as the 
training set, while GSE19234, GSE22153, and GSE65904 served as external validation 
cohorts. Models were ranked based on their concordance index (C-index) in descend­
ing order, and the model with the highest average C-index across all validation datasets 
was selected as the optimal model. Finally, the results of the validation set are presented 
using a heat map. To evaluate the accuracy of the model, we conducted a compre­
hensive literature search in PubMed 2023 in to identify existing prognostic models 
for melanoma [19]. We compared the C-index of these models with our model across 
the TCGA, GSE19234, GSE22153, and GSE65904 cohorts to validate its performance. 
Once the optimal prognostic model was established, we validated its predictive perfor­
mance in the four independent melanoma cohorts (TCGA, GSE19234, GSE22153, and 
GSE65904). Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was conducted to assess survival differences 
between high- and low-risk groups, and significance was determined using the log-rank 
test. Patients were stratified into high- and low-risk groups based on the risk scores, and 
survival curves were plotted accordingly.
Next, time-dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were gener­
ated using the “timeROC” R package to assess the model’s predictive power at 1-, 3-, 
and 5-year survival timepoints, and the area under the curve (AUC) was calculated 
to evaluate the model’s sensitivity and specificity. To further examine the distribution 
and discriminatory ability of the model in different risk groups, principal component 
analysis (PCA) was performed. Dimensionality reduction of the expression matrix of 
model-included genes was conducted to visualize the clustering patterns of patients in 
two-dimensional space, thereby demonstrating the model’s capacity to distinguish risk 
stratification.
2.4  Tumor Microenvironment (TME) Analysis
To investigate differences in the tumor microenvironment between the high- and low-
risk groups, the ESTIMATE algorithm was used to calculate the ImmuneScore, Stro­
malScore, and ESTIMATEScore for each sample, which reflect the infiltration levels of 
immune and stromal cells in tumor tissues. The analysis was conducted using the “esti­
mate” R package, and Wilcoxon tests were applied to assess statistical differences in 
TME scores between risk groups.
2.5  Immune Infiltration Analysis
To further elucidate the immune landscape across different risk groups, we employed 
multiple computational algorithms to estimate the abundance of infiltrating immune cell 
subsets in tumor samples, including CIBERSORT, TIMER, xCell, EPIC, MCPcounter,

QUANTISEQ, and ssGSEA. These methods were implemented via the “IOBR” R pack­
age, which integrates various immune deconvolution tools. Differences in immune cell 
infiltration between high- and low-risk groups were evaluated using the Wilcoxon rank-
sum test and visualized using boxplots.
2.6  GSVA Analysis of Immune-Related Pathways
To explore the potential functional differences in immune activity between the two risk 
groups, Gene Set Variation Analysis (GSVA) was conducted using immune-related gene 
sets. The GSVA algorithm, implemented via the “GSVA” R package, was applied to the 
expression data to calculate enrichment scores for immune-related pathways in each 
sample. Correlation analysis was then performed between the risk scores and GSVA 
scores, and the results were visualized using heatmaps to illustrate functional disparities 
in immune activity across risk groups.
2.7  Expression, Prognostic Relevance, GSEA, and Drug Sensitivity Analysis of SLC3A2 in 
Melanoma
To comprehensively investigate the functional role and clinical relevance of the key gene 
SLC3A2 in melanoma, we utilized the Bioinformatics-Driven Expression and Survival 
Tools (BEST) database (http://shiny.biosino.org/best/) for a series of integrative analyses. 
The BEST database compiles expression profiles, clinical information, and functional 
annotations from multiple public datasets, enabling systematic cancer gene analysis. 
First, differential expression of SLC3A2 between melanoma and normal tissues was 
assessed using the “Expression” module. Boxplots were generated, and statistical signifi­
cance was determined using the Wilcoxon test. Second, the “Survival” module was used 
to divide melanoma patients into high- and low-expression groups based on SLC3A2 
levels. Kaplan-Meier survival curves were plotted to evaluate its association with overall 
survival (OS) or progression-free survival (PFS), and statistical significance was calcu­
lated using the log-rank test. Third, the “GSEA” module was employed to conduct gene 
set enrichment analysis (GSEA) between high and low SLC3A2 expression groups. Path­
way enrichment was based on KEGG, Reactome, and HALLMARK gene sets to explore 
the biological functions and signaling pathways potentially regulated by SLC3A2. The 
results were evaluated using normalized enrichment scores (NES) and false discovery 
rates (FDR). Finally, the “Drug Sensitivity” module was used to assess the correlation 
between SLC3A2 expression and drug responsiveness. By integrating half-maximal 
inhibitory concentration (IC50) data from drug sensitivity databases such as GDSC and 
CTRP, we explored the relationship between SLC3A2 expression and drug sensitivity, 
thereby evaluating its potential as a therapeutic target.
2.8  Cell Culture and shRNA Interference Transfection
The human melanoma cell line A375 was purchased from the Cell Bank of the Chinese 
Academy of Sciences. Cells were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium (Gibco) supplemented 
with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin at 37 °C in a 
humidified incubator with 5% CO₂.
To knock down SLC3A2 expression, specific short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) target­
ing human SLC3A2 were designed and synthesized by GenePharma (Shanghai, China)

gen) following the manufacturer’s protocol.
2.9  Colony Formation Assay
After transfection, cells were seeded into 6-well plates at a density of 500 cells per well 
and cultured under standard conditions for 10–14 days until visible colonies formed. 
Cells were gently washed with PBS, fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min, and 
stained with 0.1% crystal violet for 30 min. Excess stain was removed, and cells were 
washed with PBS. Colony numbers were counted and photographed to evaluate cell pro­
liferation capacity.
2.10  Transwell Migration Assay
To assess the effect of SLC3A2 on melanoma cell migration, a Transwell assay was per­
formed using 8.0 μm pore-size inserts (Corning). A375 cells transfected with shRNA-
SLC3A2 were resuspended in serum-free medium and adjusted to 1 × 10⁵ cells/mL. A 
volume of 200 µL was added to the upper chamber, while 600 µL of RPMI-1640 medium 
containing 10% FBS was added to the lower chamber as a chemoattractant. After 24 h of 
incubation at 37 °C with 5% CO₂, non-migrated cells on the upper surface were removed 
using a cotton swab. Migrated cells on the lower surface were fixed with methanol for 
15 min and stained with 0.1% crystal violet for 30 min. After washing with PBS, five ran­
dom fields per insert were photographed under an inverted microscope, and the number 
of migrated cells was quantified.
2.11  Wound Healing Assay
Transfected cells were seeded in 6-well plates and grown to over 90% confluence. A ster­
ile pipette tip was used to create a straight scratch across the cell monolayer. Detached 
cells were removed by washing with PBS, and serum-free medium was added. Images of 
the wound area were captured at 0 and 24 h. The migration rate was calculated based on 
the change in wound width using ImageJ software to evaluate cell migratory ability.
3  Results
3.1  Single-cell atlas reveals melanoma cell heterogeneity and anoikis-related features
After t-SNE dimensionality reduction of the integrated single-cell melanoma samples, 
a total of 16 distinct cellular subpopulations were identified (Fig.  1A). Based on the 
expression of cell-type-specific marker genes, these subclusters were further annotated 
and categorized into six major cell types: melanocytes, NKT cells, endothelial cells, 
fibroblasts, myeloid cells, and cycling cells (Fig. 1B). The proportions of cell types varied 
substantially across different samples (Fig. 1C), suggesting pronounced heterogeneity in 
immune and tumor cell composition within melanoma. The accuracy of cell-type anno­
tation was validated using the expression patterns of multiple well-established marker 
genes (Fig. 1D). We next investigated the enrichment of anoikis-related gene signatures 
across different cell subpopulations and visualized their distribution at the single-cell 
level. Endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and melanocytes exhibited relatively high anoikis 
scores (Figs. 1E–G). Based on these scores, cells were classified into Anoikis_low and 
Anoikis_high groups. Compared with the Anoikis_low group, cells in the Anoikis_high 
group showed significantly greater numbers of intercellular interactions and stronger

ronment (Fig. 1I–J). Additionally, we identified 150 genes strongly associated with anoi­
kis for further downstream analyses (Fig. 1K).

3.3  Systematic Comparison of the Anoikis-Related Prognostic Model
To further validate the superiority of our constructed model, we conducted a system­
atic comparative analysis with previously published prognostic models for melanoma 
retrieved from the PubMed database. The comparison was based on the C-index rank­
ing of each model across four independent datasets (TCGA, GSE19234, GSE22153, 
and GSE65904) (Fig. 3A–D). Our model demonstrated the highest performance in the 
TCGA training set, with a C-index of 0.774, ranking first among all models (Fig. 3A). In 
the external validation cohorts, our model also exhibited strong performance, ranking 
3rd in GSE19234 (Fig. 3B), 2nd in GSE22153 (Fig. 3C), and among the top in GSE65904 
(Fig. 3D), consistently outperforming most published models and showcasing excellent 
stability and generalizability.
3.4  Tumor Microenvironment and Immune-Related Analyses
We next explored the immune landscape associated with the risk model. Immune cell 
infiltration analysis revealed a general trend of reduced immune infiltration in the high-
risk group, particularly for B cells, CD4⁺ T cells, and CD8⁺ T cells (Fig. 4A). Addition­
ally, we calculated four tumor microenvironment (TME)-related scores. Risk scores were 
significantly negatively correlated with stromal score, immune score, and ESTIMATE 
score, and positively correlated with tumor purity (Fig. 4B), suggesting a potential role of 
the model in reflecting the immunosuppressive microenvironment. Furthermore, GSVA 
correlation analysis of immune-related pathways revealed that the risk score was nega­
tively associated with several immune regulatory pathways (Fig. 5).

regulatory pathways, suggesting impaired immune responses in high-risk patients.
3.5  Identification and Validation of the Key Gene SLC3A2
Figure 6 presents the composition of the genes involved in the prognostic model. Among 
these, SLC3A2 showed the strongest positive correlation with the risk score and was 
identified as a key gene. We then explored the clinical significance of SLC3A2 using 
the BEST database. In the GSE46517 dataset, SLC3A2 was significantly overexpressed 
in melanoma tissues (Fig. 7A). In the GSE98394 dataset, its expression increased with 
higher T stage (Fig. 7B), a trend also observed in the TCGA_SKCM cohort (Fig. 7C).

4  Discussion
In this study, we presented a comprehensive multi-omics approach to elucidate the 
anoikis-related molecular landscape of melanoma and its prognostic implications. By 
integrating single-cell and bulk transcriptome datasets, we systematically dissected the 
heterogeneity of melanoma at the cellular level and revealed the enrichment of anoi­
kis-related gene signatures in distinct tumor and immune cell populations. Our find­
ings underscore the critical role of anoikis resistance in melanoma pathogenesis and its 
potential as a prognostic indicator and therapeutic target.
Anoikis resistance in stromal components, such as endothelial cells and fibroblasts, 
likely contributes to the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment [20, 21]. These 
findings suggest that targeting anoikis pathways in stromal cells may be a promising 
strategy to remodel the immune landscape in melanoma. The single-cell RNA-seq anal­
ysis revealed substantial intra-tumoral heterogeneity, with melanocytes, cycling tumor 
cells, and immune infiltrates exhibiting differential enrichment of anoikis-related genes. 
This suggests that anoikis resistance is not confined to a single cell type but may be a 
widespread adaptation mechanism in the tumor ecosystem. CellChat-based intercellular

To translate these findings into clinical utility, we employed a rigorous machine learn­
ing framework encompassing 101 algorithms and their combinations to construct a 
robust prognostic model based on 150 anoikis-correlated genes. The model demon­
strated high predictive performance across the TCGA training set and three indepen­
dent GEO validation cohorts, outperforming previously published melanoma prognostic 
models. The superior accuracy of our model, as evidenced by time-dependent ROC 
analysis and C-index comparison, underscores the power of multi-cohort validation and 
algorithmic integration in developing clinically applicable biomarkers.
In addition to risk stratification, we investigated the immune landscape associated 
with different risk groups. High-risk patients exhibited significantly lower immune and 
stromal scores, indicative of an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Immune infil­
tration analysis using multiple algorithms consistently revealed diminished infiltration 
of CD8⁺ T cells and other effector immune populations in high-risk tumors, which may 
explain their poor clinical outcomes. Moreover, GSVA identified downregulation of key 
immune pathways, including interferon responses and T cell receptor signaling, further 
supporting the link between anoikis resistance and immune evasion.
Among the genes included in the prognostic model, SLC3A2 emerged as a key driver 
with both prognostic and functional relevance. SLC3A2 encodes a component of the 
L-type amino acid transporter complex and has been implicated in nutrient uptake and 
redox balance [25, 26]. SLC3A2 has been found to be associated with resistance to anoi­
kis and tumor metastasis in Ewing’s sarcoma. This effect is achieved through interaction 
with IL-1RAP [27]. Our bioinformatic analysis demonstrated that SLC3A2 was signifi­
cantly upregulated in melanoma and associated with adverse prognosis. GSEA suggested 
its involvement in metabolic reprogramming, consistent with its known oncogenic func­
tions. Functional assays confirmed that knockdown of SLC3A2 impaired melanoma cell 
proliferation and migration, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target.
Nevertheless, our study has some limitations. First, although we integrated multiple 
datasets and validated our findings across cohorts, the retrospective nature of the analy­
sis warrants prospective validation. Second, while in vitro assays confirmed the func­
tional role of SLC3A2, further mechanistic studies are needed to delineate the signaling 
pathways through which it regulates anoikis and immune responses. Third, scRNA-seq 
was limited to a single dataset, and expanding the analysis to additional datasets may 
uncover more diverse anoikis-related cellular phenotypes.

In conclusion, our integrative analysis elucidates the heterogeneity of anoikis resis­
tance in melanoma and establishes a novel prognostic model with potential clinical util­
ity. We identify SLC3A2 as a promising therapeutic target, linking anoikis resistance 
to melanoma progression and immune modulation. These findings may inform future 
efforts in personalized therapy and immune intervention in melanoma.

Abstract: Objective Anoikis, a form of programmed cell death triggered by detachment from the extracellular matrix, plays a crucial role in metastasis and immune escape in melanoma. We aimed to identify anoikis-related prognostic markers using integrated machine learning and single-cell analysis. Methods We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing data from the GEO dataset GSE215120 and transcriptomic profiles from multiple melanoma cohorts, including TCGA, GSE19234, GSE22153, and GSE65904. Batch effects in single-cell data were corrected using the Harmony algorithm. Cell subpopulations were annotated via t-SNE dimensionality reduction and canonical markers, and AUCell was employed to compute the enrichment scores of anoikis-related genes across cell subtypes. A total of 150 anoikis-related genes were identified, and 101 machine learning algorithms and their combinations (including Cox regression, random survival forest, and gradient boosting machine) were systematically evaluated to identify the optimal prognostic model. Model performance was validated in independent cohorts using the concordance index (C-index), Kaplan–Meier survival analysis, and time-dependent ROC curves. Tumor microenvironment characteristics were assessed using ESTIMATE, CIBERSORT, and GSVA. The clinical relevance and functional role of SLC3A2 were further validated using the BEST database and in vitro experiments, including shRNA-mediated knockdown, colony formation, and Transwell migration assays. Results Single-cell analysis revealed significantly elevated anoikis scores in endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and melanocytes. High-scoring subpopulations exhibited more active cell–cell communication networks centered on endothelial cells. The “random survival forest + gradient boosting machine” model demonstrated optimal prognostic performance across the TCGA training cohort and validation cohorts (GSE19234, GSE22153, GSE65904), with a C-index of 0.774. Patients in the high-risk group had significantly shorter overall survival, and the model achieved strong predictive accuracy with AUCs ranging from 0.64 to 0.81 for 1-, 3-, and 5-year survival. Tumor microenvironment analysis indicated reduced immune infiltration (CD8⁺ T cells, B cells) in the high-risk group, suggestive of an immunosuppressive phenotype.
